issues.description: State machine collapse from 4 states to 3 (working merged into walking) is undocumented and load-bearing
issues.detail: The previous enum was unsorted | working | walking | sorted; the patch removes `working` and reuses `walking` for the 'children pushed, awaiting second visit' role. push()'s cycle-detection branch (`case walking:` using LastIndexFunc) now fires on the same state as normal in-progress descent. The reduction may be sound, but the diff asserts it by deletion rather than proving it — the new contract depends on walking being set strictly before children are pushed and never unset until sorted, and that ordering is now load-bearing without a written invariant. Several reviewers flag the rename as confusing because a node is marked `walking` while we are actually still descending, not walking back up.

issues.description: Cleanup moved into a defer changes the lifecycle/time semantics of Sorter state
issues.detail: Previously `clear(s.state)` ran at the start of Sort() (lazy reset); the new code clears state and stack inside a deferred block that runs on every exit including early yield termination and panic. This is a deliberate buffer-reuse / single-exit choice, but it complects 'finished iterating' with 'forget the result' and no caller-facing contract documents the new lifecycle. Dijkstra additionally calls the four-step deferred reset a 'smuggled goto' that hides the cleanup contract from each return site; a named cleanup function called explicitly would surface the postcondition.

issues.description: clear(s.stack) before reslicing to [:0] is either redundant or in the wrong order
issues.detail: The defer does `clear(s.stack); s.stack = s.stack[:0]`. Once the slice is resliced to zero length, the cleared entries are unreachable through s.stack and any append will overwrite them, so the clear is dead work unless the intent is to release pointer-holding Node references retained in the backing array beyond the new len — in which case the order should be reslice first, then clear the tail being released. Pick one and comment why. (Pike and Knuth treat this as merely under-documented but correct; Torvalds treats it as wrong-or-redundant.)

issues.description: Behavioral change: `s.state[k] = sorted` now only set inside the `state != sorted` branch and only after yield returns true
issues.detail: Old code unconditionally wrote sorted after the pop, even when yield returned false (early return). New code only writes sorted on the success path. With the new defer-clear this is observationally fine, but the per-key postcondition 'after pop, state[k] == sorted' no longer holds at the moment of early return, and the change is a semantic reordering buried inside what looks like a cleanup. Pike notes this also quietly fixes a pre-existing bug where early-terminated iteration left a node marked sorted; that bug fix should be called out.

issues.description: Cycle-detection branch in push() is O(stack) per repeated visit — asymptotic claim deserves audit
issues.detail: When push() is called on a node already in the walking state, it performs `slicesx.LastIndexFunc` over the entire stack. On a pathological DAG with wide fan-in to a shared ancestor this turns the overall sort from O(V+E) into roughly O(E*V). The PR does not change this, but the state rename invites scrutiny: either state the worst-case complexity in a comment or replace the linear scan with a map lookup of stack position.

issues.description: PR bundles three independent changes — refactor, bug fix, and cleanup-correctness fix — into one patch
issues.detail: The description lists (1) reduce internal states, (2) fix non-zero stack elements, (3) clear state on completion. These are three independent changes with three independent risk profiles. The state collapse is a refactor; the `s.stack[0:]` → `s.stack[:0]` change is a bug fix for what was previously a no-op reslice; the deferred state clear is a correctness fix for reuse. Land as three patches so bisect can blame the right one.

issues.description: Sort()'s contract (preconditions, postconditions, invariant, termination function) is not written down
issues.detail: Neither the patch nor the surrounding code carries a written precondition for Sort, a postcondition over the yielded sequence, or a loop invariant relating s.stack, s.state, and the unyielded portion of the DAG. Liskov and Dijkstra both argue this is the very gap that produced the bug being fixed: the invariant 'every key in s.state[walking] is currently on s.stack in DFS-discovery order; every key in s.state[sorted] has been yielded exactly once; every reachable key not in s.state is unvisited' should be stated explicitly, along with a termination function that is monotonically decreasing.

issues.description: Original `s.stack = s.stack[0:]` was a no-op typo — the reset was never actually happening
issues.detail: `s.stack[0:]` is identical to `s.stack` and does not truncate. So on a reused Sorter, the previous run's stack contents persisted across calls. The PR title implies this was a 'non-zero elements' problem; the truth is starker: the reslice did nothing. The new defer with `clear` + `[:0]` is correct. Worth calling out in the commit message that the prior line was an outright bug, not just suboptimal, and that the new invariant 'stack is empty on entry to Sort()' now depends on the prior call's defer running.

issues.description: Defer-based cleanup uses both `clear(s.stack)` and `s.stack = s.stack[:0]` — correct Go 1.21+ idiom but deserves a one-line comment
issues.detail: clear() zeroes the underlying array entries so retained Node pointers can be GC'd; the reslice resets length while preserving capacity. This is the correct pooled-slice-of-pointers idiom but a reader who hasn't internalized the semantics may try to 'simplify' it to one line. A one-line literate comment would prevent regression.

issues.description: Comment rewrite contains typos ('visisted', 'if its') and is vaguer than what it replaces
issues.detail: The new comment reads 'whether this node has been visisted and if its the first or second visit'. 'visisted' should be 'visited'; 'its' should be 'it's'. More importantly, this is the load-bearing explanation of the two-pass DFS now that the state machine is more implicit, and it should name the three states (unsorted, walking, sorted) and the transition triggers rather than gesture at them.

issues.description: No test added to demonstrate the state-reuse bug being fixed
issues.detail: The PR title is 'Fix state reuse' but the diff contains no test exercising back-to-back Sort() calls on a reused Sorter, nor a test exercising early termination via yield returning false followed by a subsequent Sort(). A regression that motivated the patch should be expressible as a failing test on the old code; without one, future refactors will reintroduce the bug silently.

issues.description: Sorter struct complects allocation pool, traversal state, and re-entrancy guard
issues.detail: The Sorter holds (a) reusable allocations (`state` map, `stack` slice), (b) the in-progress traversal of one Sort call, and (c) an `iterating` flag for re-entrancy. The bug existed because (a) and (b) were entangled — 'reset for new sort' and 'free buffers after sort' were the same operation, done in the wrong place, with a typo no test caught. A cleaner decomposition: traversal state local to the iterator closure; Sorter is only the pool. Not blocking, but the shape is what allowed the bug.

issues.description: Eliminating the intermediate state is a good-taste structural simplification, if naming gets fixed
issues.detail: The two-visit DFS pattern doesn't actually need a separate 'children pushed' state because the stack itself encodes 'have we descended yet'. Collapsing it is the right instinct; the execution only falls down on naming, since a node is marked `walking` while we are descending rather than walking back. A name like `onStack` or `entered`/`exited` would be more honest.

dissents.topic: Is `clear(s.stack)` before `s.stack = s.stack[:0]` correct, redundant, or wrong-ordered?

positions.position: Either dead work or in the wrong order: once you reslice to zero length the cleared entries are unreachable. If the goal is to release Node pointers retained in the backing array beyond the new len, reslice first and clear the tail. As written, pick one and comment why.

Correct Go 1.21+ idiom for a pooled slice holding pointers — clear zeroes entries so Nodes can be GC'd, the reslice keeps capacity. Just under-documented; add a one-line comment so a future maintainer doesn't 'simplify' it.
Both calls are needed — clear() for GC of node references and the reslice for length — so the pattern is correct, merely under-documented.

Treats the cleanup as right-shaped overall (defer with clear+[:0] is the correct fix), but argues the deeper problem is that the Sorter complects pool and traversal state; ordering is not the central issue.

dissents.topic: Severity and framing of the state-machine collapse (working → walking)

positions.position: Good-taste structural simplification — the intermediate state was unnecessary because the stack itself encodes 'have we descended'. The fault is naming: `walking` is now a lie because the node is being descended into, not walked back up.

The data structure now carries less information than the algorithm needs to express itself clearly — the reader must reason about temporal ordering to see why one state covers both 'expanding' and 'revisit'. Push()'s cycle-detection conflation is load-bearing behavior change disguised as a rename.

The collapse is asserted by deletion rather than proved. The author owes a one-paragraph proof that no caller or internal branch can distinguish the two former states, in particular that walking is set strictly before children are pushed and never unset until sorted.
Plausibly correct but the diff doesn't show enough context to confirm safety; the commit message should explain why the two phases are actually one.
Plausible but under-audited; state the invariant inline ('walking == node is on stack with children being expanded') so the O(n) push() scan has a stated correctness argument.
Substitutability of the type is preserved; the issue is that the state machine of the ADT is part of its contract and is nowhere written down.

dissents.topic: Is the defer-based cleanup the right shape, or a smuggled goto?

positions.position: The defer-based cleanup is the right shape: single exit point, all state cleared in one place.

The deferred four-step reset (clear state, clear stack, reslice, unset iterating) is a smuggled goto that hides the cleanup contract from each return site. A named cleanup function called explicitly at each exit would make the postcondition visible.
Reasonable buffer-reuse choice but it complects 'finished iterating' with 'forget the result' — worth verifying no caller depends on post-sort inspection of s.state.
Couples state lifecycle to iteration in a way the type spec does not promise; needs an explicit decision on whether cleanup is an invariant of Sort() the function or of completed iteration.

synthesis.summary: All six reviewers converge on a single verdict: the fix is moving in the right direction (the previous `s.stack = s.stack[0:]` was a no-op that left stale state, and deferring cleanup is correct) but the patch arrives under-specified — bundling a refactor (4 states → 3), a bug fix (no-op reslice → real reset), and a correctness fix (clearing state on completion) into one commit with no regression test and a typo'd comment ('visisted', 'if its'). The strongest preserved disagreement is over `clear(s.stack)` before `s.stack[:0]`: Torvalds reads it as either dead work or wrong-ordered and demands a decision, while Knuth, Pike, and Hickey read it as the correct Go 1.21+ pooled-slice idiom that is merely under-documented. A second live disagreement is whether the deferred four-step cleanup is the right shape (Pike: yes, single exit point) or a 'smuggled goto' hiding the postcondition from each return site (Dijkstra). A third tension is how strongly to insist on a written invariant and proof for the state-machine collapse: Dijkstra and Liskov require it; Torvalds and Pike want better naming and a comment; Knuth wants the asymptotic claim audited for push()'s O(stack) cycle-detection scan. Recommended path: split the patch into three commits, name the surviving state honestly, write down the invariant and termination function above Sort(), proofread the comment, and add a Sort-twice regression test before merge.
